extracted.intended_audience: readers and writers interested in narrative technique and digressive 18th-century fiction (general literary audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Meta-reflections and informal guidance embedded in Tristram Shandy about composing digressive, satirical novels: persistence in composition, permitted digressions, timeliness, avoidance of rote/scaffolded instruction, and ensuring claims are substantiated. Useful for authors of long, episodic, or self-conscious fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing is warfare; success depends on resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: The life of a writer, whatever he might fancy to the contrary, was not so much a state of composition, as a state of warfare; and his probation in it... both depending alike, not half so much upon the degrees of his wit—as his RESISTANCE.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persistence and the capacity to resist obstacles (internal and external) matter more to the writer's progress than sheer wit. Treat composition as a prolonged struggle where steady resistance advances the work; an anti-pattern is expecting inspiration/wit alone to carry a project through.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid letting prejudices of education dominate the book
rubrics_metrics.description: Prejudice of education, he would say, is the devil,—and the multitudes of them which we suck in with our mother’s milk—are the devil and all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not allow received ideas, clichés, or conventional schooling to dictate your writing. If a writer submits tamely to what 'prejudice' obtrudes, the result will be a 'farrago of the clack of nurses, and of the nonsense of the old women.' Strive for original judgement rather than parroting inherited opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness: delays can render earlier material useless
rubrics_metrics.description: He was three years, and something more, indefatigably at work, and, at last, had scarce completed... the misfortune was, that I was all that time totally neglected... and what was almost as bad, by the very delay, the first part of the work, upon which my father had spent the most of his pains, was rendered entirely useless,—every day a page or two became of no consequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long delays in composition or publication may make previously written pages obsolete or irrelevant. Keep awareness of timeliness and the ongoing context of your work; pacing and forward progress preserve the usefulness of early material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted digression: go backwards/forwards if you keep the story's line
rubrics_metrics.description: ’TIS a point settled...—that provided he keeps along the line of his story,—he may go backwards and forwards as he will,—’tis still held to be no digression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Digressions are acceptable (even encouraged) so long as they remain, in some sense, connected to the central line or purpose of the story. The narrator may roam in time or topic, provided the overarching thread is respected; aim to make digressions feel purposeful rather than aimless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find wit and instruction in everything, but avoid hollow scaffold-work
rubrics_metrics.description: Every thing in this world... is big with jest, and has wit in it, and instruction too,—if we can but find it out. —Here is the scaffold work of INSTRUCTION, its true point of folly, without the BUILDING behind it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek humorous and instructive material in ordinary events, yet ensure there is substantive 'building' behind playful scaffolding. Avoid producing content that is mere surface ornament or rote scaffolding without deeper insight; the balance of jest and genuine instruction strengthens writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convey wisdom, not mere rote learning
rubrics_metrics.description: SCIENCES MAY BE LEARNED BY ROTE BUT WISDOM NOT.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't mistake memorized facts or formulae for real insight. In exposition or characterization, aim to communicate understanding and judgement, not only catalogued knowledge. An anti-pattern is relying on rote recitation (e.g., pedantic lists) in place of reflective commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edit out or skip prefatory/dry matter that isn't closely connected
rubrics_metrics.description: The first thirty pages... are a little dry; and as they are not closely connected with the subject,—for the present we'll pass them by: ’tis a prefatory introduction... upon political or civil government...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to omit, condense, or defer prefaces and material that are tangential or dry. Respect the reader's attention: if sections are not closely connected to the central subject or are sluggish, consider cutting or postponing them to maintain momentum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect the reader's impatience; keep the narrative moving
rubrics_metrics.description: Time presses upon me,—my reader is impatient—I must get forwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain narrative pace and avoid excessive preliminaries that frustrate readers. Signal when you will return to digressions later, but prioritize forward movement of the plot or central argument to sustain engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantiate grand claims—avoid hollow theses
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole secret of health depending upon the due contention betwixt the radical heat and the radical moisture... and that he had managed the point so well, that there was not one single word wet or dry upon radical heat or radical moisture, throughout the whole chapter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not make sweeping or emphatic claims unless the text actually develops them. Avoid the anti-pattern of asserting a bold thesis and then failing to provide substance or argument; readers expect claims to be supported by relevant content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use morals/anecdotes sparingly and with economy
rubrics_metrics.description: A great MORAL might be picked handsomely out of this, but I have not time—’tis enough to say, wherever the demolition began, ’twas equally fatal to the sash window.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may extract morals or larger meanings from incidents, but brevity can be effective. Over-moralizing or long-winded elaboration on a small event can bog the narrative; concise remark often suffices to point the lesson without stalling the story.
